newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC playing safe on quotas.
newsitem.headline: OPEC playing safe on quotas.

text.p: OPEC was set Wednesday to take traders' advice and not tamper with its oil export quotas amid uncertainty on how winter weather may affect the demand for heating oil.
There was also concern about the impact of the timing of Iraq's re-entry as an exporter.

Delegates at the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries' 101st ministerial conference predicted that the cartel would go along with a Saudi Arabian-led consensus of extending current output quotas, despite rampant violations among the 11 members, at least until June 1997.
Ministers who favour a "rollover" included Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh, although he also indicated concern about the problem of members exceeding their export limits.
"I suppose ... it is best to keep the current ceiling. It depends on us all being very careful," he said.

Traders say OPEC would be best advised to sidestep issues of market share and alleged cheating, to avoid any public haggling that might alarm skittish oil markets and jeopardise this year's rally in prices.

In early trading Wednesday, crude oil was up 19 cents at $23.81 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, while in London, oil hovered at $22.75 a barrel, compared with only $18 back in June when OPEC last met.

Prices have risen because of depleted inventories of heating fuel ahead of winter, despite the revived prospect that the 1990 Gulf War ban on Iraqi exports may soon be relaxed and OPEC's own quota violations.

Alleged export excess by Venezuela and others is said by Western monitors to have pushed OPEC output million barrels a day above the ceiling of 25.03 million barrels per day, even before the 800,000 barrels per day that Iraq plans to export under a United Nations food-for-oil deal to ease the Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil sales.

But delegates say that OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia and its Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates feel that the market can absorb even more oil, because stocks are low. They also cite the delay so far in the resumption of Iraqi sales.

Iraq's chief delegate to the OPEC meeting, which may end on Thursday, told reporters he hoped his country's oil would flow within weeks. The official, Osama al-Hiti, said that only the pricing formula and "very minor technicalities" had to be ironed out.
Depending on its severity, the winter can swing oil demand by a million barrels daily, Barclays Bank economists said in their latest Commodities Survey.
Barclays has revised up its forecast for average 1996 oil prices to $20 per barrel from only $16.80 in 1995. But they noted that "our view remains that prices are likely to ease next year."

The expectation that prices will be weaker by perhaps $1 a barrel is based on the "strong possibility" of revived Iraqi exports and a prospect of increased supply from the North Sea, Asia and Latin America.
